title: Seen: Hanuman's first word
hook: Hanuman has the biggest news of Rama's life, and he chooses his first word with care
carry: vak tapas: speech that's true, kind and calming

segments.voice: Yesterday: the return. Jambavan left the rescue to Rama, the monkeys raided the honey forest, and your line was svadharma, do your own part, offer the rest.

Rama has been waiting on a mountain outside Kishkindha. The search parties from the north, the east and the west have already come back with nothing. Now the southern party arrives, loud and happy, and Hanuman steps forward. He has crossed the sea, found her, spoken with her, fought half of Lanka and left it burning. He has a long, astonishing story to tell. And first he has to decide which word comes out of his mouth.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, AND NO NEWS.` → `THREE PARTIES CAME BACK EMPTY.` → `WHICH WORD FIRST?`

segments.voice: The word he puts first, in Valmiki's Sanskrit, is drishta. Seen. He bows and tells Rama the queen has been seen, that she is keeping her vows, that she is unharmed. Think about the order. If he had begun with the ocean, or Lanka, or the words I went, Rama would have spent every sentence waiting, heart in his throat. If he had begun with her name alone, Rama might have braced for the worst. Seen comes first, and the fear is answered before it can rise. The Tamil poet Kamban, retelling the story, makes it even sharper: his Hanuman opens with the Tamil for I saw, before he names her at all. Only then does Hanuman tell the rest: the leap, the city at night, the ashoka grove, a thin woman under a tree, Ravana's threats, Rama's own ring passed down through the branches. Joy comes over Rama and Lakshmana as they listen. Sugriva had already guessed, from the monkeys' wild celebration on the way home. Hindus have a name for this kind of care. The Bhagavad Gita calls it the tapas, the discipline, of speech: words that are true, kind and helpful, and that don't stir up fear. Speech is part of your spiritual practice, not just your manners. And Hanuman is its great example. When Rama first met him in the forest, he told Lakshmana he'd never heard anyone speak so well. Here, with the biggest news of Rama's life, Hanuman proves it: before he speaks, he thinks about where his words will land.
screen: `DRISHTA: SEEN.` · `THE FEAR ANSWERED FIRST.` · `KAMBAN'S HANUMAN: I SAW.` · then, large: `VAK TAPAS: THE DISCIPLINE OF SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep mauna, a short stretch of silence, as part of their practice. Sit in mauna now for a few breaths. Then think of one piece of news you'll bring someone soon, and try the Gita's test: is it true, is it kind, does it help, will it ease their fear rather than raise it? Find the first word that answers their fear. If you pray, offer your words before you speak them.
Seen. Drishta in Sanskrit. Hanuman's first word to Rama, put first on purpose, so the fear is over before the story begins.
Your line: vak tapas, speech that's true, kind and calming. Tomorrow, what he carried back in his hand. Day six hundred thirty-two, done.

howItsDone: Ramayana teachers, in temples and in family readings, often pause on Hanuman's first word, seen, as a lesson in the Gita's discipline of speech; Kamban's Tamil Ramayana gives the same moment as I saw.

notes: The index word is the title's head, written exactly as the index gives it ("seen, with the opening quotation mark); the outline may want the word set to seen or dṛṣṭā.
Valmiki's exact wording of the first report (dṛṣṭā devī / dṛṣṭā sīteti) and its sarga in the vulgate numbering: confirm. The script says only that drishta, seen, comes first.
Kamban's Hanuman opening with kaṇṭaṉeṉ (I saw) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the reference and the twelfth-century dating.
Rama waits on Mount Prasravana near Kishkindha; the script says only 'a mountain outside Kishkindha'.
Sugriva's guess (from the monkeys' wild celebration in the honey grove) is told briefly; day 631 tells it in full, so this is a one-line recap.
